l: the earth-born warriors, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The earth-born warriors are a race of armed men, brothers newly sprung from the earth. They arise from the dragon's teeth as a crop, become maddened, and kill one another in civil war, leaving five survivors: Chthonius, Udeus, Hyperenor, Pelor, and Echion. In the concluding interpretation, they are people of the country or soldiers won by Cadmus, who assist him in conquering enemies and building Thebes's citadel.

l: the five surviving earth-born warriors, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Five survivors of the earth-born warriors survive the fighting, lay down arms and exchange assurances of brotherly concord, then assist Cadmus in building the city.

l: the dragon's death, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_caused_by Cadmus The dragon's death comes after Cadmus wounds it with his spear and pursues it as it retreats. He presses the spear through its throat until the dragon's neck is pierced together with the trunk of an oak.

l: the dragon's sowing, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_performed_by Cadmus [on Minerva's advice] Cadmus performs the dragon's sowing by opening a furrow with a plough and scattering the dragon's teeth on the ground. The teeth immediately produce armed earth-born warriors.

l: the earth-born warriors' civil war, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_fought_by the earth-born warriors [with mutual wounds] The earth-born warriors' civil war begins when one of them strikes a brother with a sword after telling Cadmus not to engage in civil war. The warriors then kill one another with swords and darts until only five remain.

l: the building of Thebes, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_ordered_by the oracle of Phoebus The building of Thebes is carried out by Cadmus with the five surviving earth-born warriors as his associates. The city is built according to the order of the oracle of Phœbus.

l: Amphion, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Amphion, Niobe’s husband and ruler of Thebes, fathers seven sons and seven daughters with her. After witnessing his children’s destruction, he kills himself in grief; he and his entire race are described as extinct, and people mourn him.

l: Hermione, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Hermione, also called Harmonia, is described as the daughter of Mars and Venus and wife of Cadmus. She accompanies Cadmus into exile and retirement in Illyria. As he changes into a serpent, she laments, asks the celestial Gods to transform her too, and becomes a serpent; other accounts call her a singing girl or link her name to Mount Hermon.

l: Cadmus's soldiers, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Cadmus’s soldiers, symbolized by dragon’s teeth and earth-born warriors, wear helmets and armor, carry brass-pointed darts, help him conquer enemies, and establish Thebes.

l: Diana's Nymphs, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Diana's Nymphs are bathing attendants who assist Diana with her equipment, clothing, hair, and water, then shriek and surround her to cover her bodies when Actæon arrives.

l: Nephele, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Nephele, Athamas’s wife and mother of Phryxus and Helle, is divorced; afterward Ino seeks to destroy her children.

l: Gargaphie, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Gargaphie is a pitch-tree and cypress-filled valley sacred to Diana, whose secluded recess contains a natural grotto and clear fountain for her post-hunt bathing.

l: Actæon’s dogs, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Actæon’s dogs are a pack of hunting dogs, said to number fifty though lists differ. After Actæon is transformed into a stag, they pursue, wound, and tear apart their master without recognizing him, urged on by his companions. Named members include Melampus, Ladon, Tigris, Thoüs, and Lycisca. According to Apollodorus, they later die of grief.

l: Actæon’s transformation, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Actæon’s transformation is a punishment in the Actæon fable, caused by Diana after he sees her bathing. Diana’s avenging water changes him into a fearful, spotted stag with horns and altered limbs. Though his understanding remains, he cannot speak as a man; notes also give nonliteral alternatives involving his dogs or ruined hunting establishment.

l: Actæon’s death, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Actæon’s death is the killing of Actæon by his own hunting dogs, which surround him and bury their jaws in his body while his companions keep seeking him. Some accounts say the dogs became mad; Apollodorus places the death on Mount Cithæron after Actæon saw Diana bathing.

l: Diana bathing, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Diana bathing is an accidental encounter and bathing scene in Diana’s bathing grotto. It begins when Actæon wanders unknowingly into the place and sees Diana without her garments; curiosity draws him nearer, and Diana’s punishment transforms him.

l: hunting, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_a activity [pursuit of wild beasts] Actæon and his companions hunt through a mountain marked by the blood of wild beasts. After the day's sport, Actæon orders the men to stop, remove the nets, and resume the hunt on the following morning.

l: Gargaphie grotto, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Natural arch-like pumice and light sand-stone grotto in a secluded grove, with Gargaphie fountain on its right; Diana bathes there after hunting.

l: Agave, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Agave, daughter of Cadmus and mother of Pentheus, is a Bacchante on Mount Cithæron. In frenzy, she strikes Pentheus, helps tear him apart, and raises his severed head in claimed victory.

l: Athamas, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Athamas, son of Aeolus and great-grandson of Deucalion, is a husband and father whose marriages and madness shape his story. He marries Ino, divorces Nephele, later remarries Nephele, and is also described as taking Ino back; he fathers Learchus and Melicerta with Ino and Phryxus and Helle. During famine at Thebes he orders consultation of the oracle of Delphi. After discovering Ino’s deceit, and while maddened by Tisiphone’s poison, he pursues Ino, kills Learchus, and pursues Melicerta. After Phryxus’s death, Æetes seizes his treasures.

l: Actæon fable, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Actæon’s transformation is a fable attributed most probably to Diana Britomartis: Diana punishes Actæon after he sees her naked, with accounts differing between transformation and death by mad dogs, financial ruin from hounds, or offenses involving Diana or Semele.

l: Greek mythology, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Greek mythology is presented through differing accounts of Niobe’s family and the deaths of her children, interpreted through natural or historical events such as plague and the destructive powers of Apollo and Diana. It is also proposed to derive partly from Egyptian notions of the future state and from real places, animals, plants, and customs.

l: Beroë, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Beroë is the Epidaurian nurse of Semele; Juno assumes her old-woman form to deceive Semele, while Iris and Georgics also mention forms or persons of that name.

l: the pregnancy of Semele, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: comes_from Jupiter's seed Semele's pregnancy by Jupiter intensifies Juno's anger. Juno views it as evidence of Jupiter's crime and resents that Semele is about to become a mother by him.

l: Juno's revenge, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Juno's revenge consists of deceiving Semele into asking Jupiter to appear in his full divine splendor. She intends for Semele to be destroyed by the consequences of that request.

l: intrigue between Semele and Jupiter, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The intrigue between Semele and Jupiter, characterized by Juno as a stolen embrace, probably gave occasion to the Fable and ended tragically.

l: Jupiter's oath, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_an_oath_by the Stygian stream [invoked as witness] Jupiter's oath is sworn by the Styx, which he calls the dread stream and the God of the Gods. Because he has sworn to grant Semele whatever she chooses, he cannot withdraw from her request.

l: death of Semele and her son, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Pausanias says that Semele and her son were thrown into the sea by Cadmus. They were cast ashore at Oreate, where Semele was buried.

l: Fable, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The Fable most probably arose from a tragic intrigue between Semele and one of the princes called Jupiter. Its later account includes Semele's elevation among the Goddesses after Bacchus brought her from hell to heaven.

l: Nyseian Nymphs, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Nyseian Nymphs, named Cysseis, Nysa, Erato, Eryphia, Bromia, and Polyhymnia, possess Nyseian caves and brought up Bacchus in Nysa.

l: Typhœus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Typhœus is a Giant who aspires to Heaven and is involved in the war of the Gods with the Giants. Defeated by the Gods, he is buried beneath Trinacria and Ætna, with his limbs pinned under Pelorus, Pachynus, and Lilybœum. He struggles to rise, casts out sand and flame, and his efforts are believed to cause fires and earthquakes.

l: Semele's burning, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_caused_by Jupiter's lightning [during Jupiter's manifestation] Semele's mortal body is unable to withstand Jupiter's divine lightning, and she is burned to ashes in his presence.

l: Bacchus's premature birth, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_a premature birth [of Bacchus] The infant Bacchus is removed from Semele's womb before he is fully formed. He is inserted into Jupiter's thigh and completes there the time he would otherwise have spent in the womb.

l: Tiresias's transformation, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_caused_by staff [when he strikes the serpents] Tiresias changes from a man into a woman after striking two serpents that are coupling in a green wood. Seven years later, he strikes the serpents again and returns to his original sex and shape.

l: dispute over sexual pleasure, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Jupiter claims that females receive greater sexual pleasure than males, while Juno denies it. Tiresias, who has experienced both sexes, is asked to decide the dispute and confirms Jupiter's claim.

l: Tiresias's blindness, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_caused_by Juno's punishment of Tiresias [for confirming Jupiter's words] Tiresias is condemned to eternal darkness after confirming Jupiter's opinion in the dispute over sexual pleasure. Jupiter later compensates him by granting knowledge of things to come.

l: Juno's punishment of Tiresias, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Juno punishes Tiresias for confirming Jupiter's claim by condemning his eyes to eternal darkness. Jupiter cannot reverse the act of another deity, so he alleviates the punishment by giving Tiresias prophetic knowledge.

l: the prophecy about Narcissus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: A prophet’s prediction says Narcissus will reach mature old age only if he never recognizes himself; initially dismissed as frivolous, it is later confirmed by his novel frenzy and manner of death.

l: Narcissus's death, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Narcissus's death follows his prolonged wasting from love and ends his sorrows. His Naiad sisters and the Dryads mourn him, while Echo resounds with their lamentations.

l: Echo's love for Narcissus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: increases from the mortification of her refusal Echo fell in love with Narcissus after seeing him drive timid stags into his nets. Her love grew stronger as she followed him and suffered his refusal. After he rejected her, she remained hidden in the woods, while her love continued.

l: Echo's voice, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Echo's voice can only repeat others' last words, answering Narcissus at first; after Echo's body wastes away and her bones become stones, it alone remains alive, heard but unseen in mountains and woods.

l: extraordinary phenomenon, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_explained_by fable [the poets probably invented the fable for this purpose] The extraordinary phenomenon is the echo, understood as the sound of people’s own voices returning to them. The poets may have invented the fable to explain this phenomenon.

l: fable, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: A fable about Echo and Pan, likely invented to explain an extraordinary phenomenon, is explained through natural philosophy or history and embellished with Echo’s parentage and Pan’s love.

l: natural philosophy, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Natural philosophy, with principles unknown to the ancients, is suggested as the foundation for explanations of the story of Leucothoë and Clytie involving frankincense and sunflower.

l: the clear spring, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: A clear, silver-like spring with unsullied water remains untouched by shepherds, animals, birds, and falling branches, shaded by grass and wood, until it reflects Narcissus's form.

l: Narcissus's reflection, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: A shadow without substance, Narcissus's reflection appears in a clear spring as a beautiful body, mirrors him, deceives his eyes, and retreats or distorts whenever the water is disturbed.

l: Narcissus flower, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: After Narcissus's body disappears, a yellow flower with white leaves is found at the funeral site, bears his name, and commonly grows around graves.

l: Narcissus's love, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Narcissus’s self-love begins with an unrecognized reflection, brings pleasure and torment, consumes his strength, and ends by causing his death.

l: Narcissus's story, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: A moral lesson showing self-love’s fatal effects: Narcissus pursues an image that continually withdraws, likened to the limited reality of eagerly pursued pleasures.

l: self-love, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: has_effects fatal [as disclosed by the fable] Self-love is portrayed as having potentially fatal effects, as illustrated by Narcissus’s pursuit of his own image.

l: Henna, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Henna, also called Enna, is a city in central Sicily, near Pergus, its lake, and a flower-filled grove. Regarded as Sicily’s navel, it is chiefly marked by prominent worship of Ceres and by springs, lakes, groves, flowers, and a cavern linked to Proserpina’s abduction while gathering flowers.

l: Acœtes, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Acœtes is a humble Mæonian sailor, pilot, and attendant of Bacchus who survives when his fellow sailors are transformed into dolphins. Captured before Pentheus, he recounts Bacchus’s punishment of the deceptive crew; Pentheus orders torture, but Acœtes’s chains fall away and the prison opens.

l: Acrisius, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Acrisius, son of Abas and king of Argos, opposes Bacchus. Fearing a prediction that Danaë’s child would kill him, he confines Danaë, then exposes her and Perseus in a boat.

l: Bacchantes, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The Bacchantes are votaries of Bacchus who celebrate his rites in frantic processions on Mount Cithæron, using ritual objects and instruments. When Pentheus watches profanely, they pursue, attack, and tear him apart in a frenzy; Agave and Autonoë are among them.

l: Naxos, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Naxos, the most famous island of the Cyclades, is sacred to Bacchus; shipwrecked mariners near it were transformed, possibly for neglecting or contempting his mysteries.

l: Bacchus festivals, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Bacchus festivals are religious rites celebrated by Bacchus’s worshippers and prescribed by a priest. They spread through Greece, drawing matrons, maids, newly married women, men, and people of every rank. Participants wear skins or vine leaves, loosen and crown their hair, carry the god’s image and green thyrsi, offer frankincense, and use ivy and nebrides. Processions, ecstatic music, cries, shouts, tambourines, cymbals, pipes, Bacchanals, Satyrs, and Silenus accompany the rites. Greek additions include licentious ceremonies; opposition is met with reported miracles and punishments, while Pentheus’s intrusion ends in destruction.

l: Pentheus’s dismemberment, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_caused_by Bacchantes [including Agave] Pentheus’s dismemberment fulfills Tiresias’s prophecy. Agave first wounds him, Autonoë and Ino tear away his arms, and Agave and the other Bacchantes rip his body apart and remove his head.

l: Tiresias’s prophecy, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Tiresias’s prophecy warns that refusing Bacchus a temple will bring Bacchus to Greece and cause Pentheus’s dismemberment, ultimately fulfilled by Pentheus’s mother and Bacchantes.

l: Bacchus’s arrival in Greece, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_followed_by Bacchic rites Bacchus enters Greece in triumph as the new god Liber, and his arrival is marked by public processions, music, dancing, and unfamiliar rites. Pentheus attempts to suppress his worship, but Bacchus’s rites prevail and are eventually honored by the matrons of Thebes.

l: Lydia, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_associated_with Etruria [colonists were said to have proceeded from Lydia to its coasts] Lydia is associated with Tantalus and Niobe, and Mount Sipylus is located there. Niobe was said to have retired to Lydia after the deaths of her husband and children.

l: Trieterica, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_a festival celebrated every three years [in honor of Bacchus] The Trieterica was a festival celebrated every three years in honor of Bacchus. During it, Bacchantes carried the figure of the god in a chariot drawn by tigers or panthers, ran around it with thyrsi, and shouted his names while playing tambourines and brazen instruments.

l: Bacchus's worship, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: originated_as worship of Osiris [its worship passed from Egypt to Greece and was altered there] Bacchic worship included mysteries, ecstatic rites, thyrsi, tambourines, vine and ivy imagery, and cries such as “Evoë. Bacche!” Greek additions to the Egyptian-derived ceremonial were described as involving licentious practices and serious offenses, which were repeatedly suppressed and re-established.

l: three daughters of Minyas, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The daughters of Minyas are women who reject Bacchus’s orgies and worship. During his festival, they stay indoors at textile work, carding, spinning, weaving, and directing handmaids, and tell stories, including Pyramus and Thisbe. As they continue to despise Bacchus and desecrate the festival, fires and light drive them to hide in the smoking house; they gain membranes and wings, lose their former shape, and become small night-flying creatures, said to be bats. Another account suggests secret death or flight instead.

l: Minyas, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Minyas is a king of the Bœotians, associated with their name Minyæ, and has daughters. Accounts conflict over whether Orchomenus was his father or his son.

l: Dercetis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Dercetis, also called Atergatis, is a Syrian goddess. Said to be Semiramis’s mother, she was represented as woman above and fish below; after drowning near Ascalon, she was said to become a fish, and a nearby temple marked the place.

l: Semiramis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Semiramis, associated with Babylon as builder of its brick walls, was said to have consecrated a temple near Hieropolis to her mother, Dercetis, rather than Juno.

l: Babylon, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Babylon is a lofty, magnificent city, said to be enclosed by Semiramis's sun-dried brick walls cemented with bitumen. Its walls are reported as 60 miles in compass, 87 feet thick, and 350 feet high. It is the setting where Pyramus and Thisbe live in adjoining houses.

l: lovers' meeting, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_at tomb of Ninus [beneath the shade of a tree] Pyramus and Thisbe arrange to meet at night outside the city, at the tomb of Ninus beneath a mulberry tree. Thisbe arrives first, but the meeting is disrupted when she flees from a lioness.

l: tomb of Ninus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The tomb of Ninus is the agreed meeting place of Pyramus and Thisbe. It stands beneath the shade of a lofty mulberry tree near a cold spring.

l: mulberry tree, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: has mulberry fruit's transformation [fruit changes from white to dark purple] The mulberry tree near the tomb of Ninus initially bears snow-white fruit. After Pyramus's blood reaches it, the tree's fruit becomes dark or purple, and it later shades the bodies of both lovers.

l: lioness, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: A lioness, jaws blood-stained after slaughter of oxen, drinks at a spring and tears Thisbe's veil as Thisbe flees.

l: Thisbe's veil, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_stained_with blood [after being torn by the lioness] Thisbe drops her veil while fleeing from the lioness. The lioness tears it and stains it with blood, and Pyramus later finds it and mistakes it for evidence that Thisbe has been killed.

l: Pyramus's sword, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: belongs_to Pyramus [worn at his side] Pyramus uses the sword with which he is girt to plunge into his bowels. After he draws it from the wound, Thisbe uses the same bloodied sword to kill herself.

l: Pyramus and Thisbe's love, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Pyramus and Thisbe’s love grows between neighbors despite forbidden marriage; they communicate through a wall crack and arrange a secret meeting at Ninus’s tomb.

l: Pyramus's suicide, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_caused_by Thisbe's veil [mistaken as proof of her death] Pyramus believes that the bloodied veil proves Thisbe has died and blames himself for her supposed death. He kisses the veil, wounds himself with his sword, and dies beneath the mulberry tree.

l: Thisbe's suicide, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: uses Pyramus's sword [after finding Pyramus dead] Thisbe finds Pyramus dying beneath the mulberry tree and declares that love and her own hand will give her strength to follow him. She plunges into the sword that is still reeking with Pyramus's blood.

l: Pyramus and Thisbe's deaths and burial, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: are_shared_by Pyramus and Thisbe [their remains are placed in one urn] Pyramus dies after stabbing himself, and Thisbe dies by the same sword after finding him. Their prayers move the gods and their parents, and what remains of them after the funeral pyre is placed in the same urn.

l: mulberry fruit's transformation, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: changes_color_to black [when fully ripened after the bloodshed] The mulberry fruit is changed by Pyramus's blood from white to a dark or purple color. It remains black when fully ripe as a memorial to the blood and fate of both lovers.

l: festival of Bacchus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The festival of Bacchus, held at night in Rhodope every three years, commemorates Bacchus's Indian expedition; it begins with desecration by Minyas's daughters, whose contempt brings punishment.

l: Shakspere, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: created Midsummer Night’s Dream [an admirable travesty of the story of Pyramus and Thisbe] Shakspere created an admirable travesty of the story of Pyramus and Thisbe in Midsummer Night’s Dream.

l: Midsummer Night’s Dream, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_a travesty [of the story of Pyramus and Thisbe] Midsummer Night’s Dream contains Shakspere’s travesty of the story of Pyramus and Thisbe.

l: Pyramus and Thisbe, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Pyramus and Thisbe is a Babylon-set moral tale, known to Ovid and Hyginus, contrasting strongly and affectingly with the loves of Mars and Venus; it warns young people against rash engagements and parents against rigorous resentment.

l: the adultery of Venus with Mars, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The Sun is the first to see the adultery of Venus with Mars and reports it to Vulcan. Vulcan exposes the lovers by trapping them in invisible chains while they are together in bed.

l: the discovery of Venus and Mars's affair, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The Sun discovers Venus and Mars’s affair, reveals their meeting place to Vulcan, and prompts Vulcan to bind and publicly expose them before the gods, who laugh. A historical version has Helius obtain proof of a court lady’s intrigue and punish the courtier.

l: Leucothoë's love affair with the Sun, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The Sun’s intense love affair with Leucothoë begins when Venus retaliates: he enters her chamber disguised as her mother, reveals himself, and Leucothoë submits to his embrace, while his devotion provokes Clytie’s enduring envy.

l: Orchamus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Orchamus rules the Achæmenian cities as a king of Persia, seventh in descent from Belus and in the stated line from Achæmenes. Identified as Leucothoë’s father, he buries her alive and may have introduced the frankincense tree into his kingdom; ancient writers otherwise mention him only here.

l: Venus's revenge on the Sun, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Venus, driven by the discovery of her affair with Mars, revenges herself on the Sun for exposing it by making him love Leucothoë, disrupting his gaze, course, winter hours, and light.

l: Colchis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Colchis is Æetes’s land, a refuge for Phryxus and destination of Jason and the Argonauts seeking the Golden Fleece. Its people witness Jason’s labors; with Medea’s aid, Jason enters, succeeds, and removes Æetes’s treasures.

l: the conjunction of Mars and Venus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: produces an amorous temperament [in persons born under it] Plutarch says that people born under the conjunction of Mars and Venus are naturally of an amorous temperament. Their indiscretions are discovered quickly if the Sun does not happen to be at a distance.

l: the discovery of the intrigue, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_explained_by Plutarch [in ‘How to read the Poets’] The discovery is attributed to the Sun in the fable. In Palæphatus’s historical explanation, Helius enters the lady’s apartment at night, obtains ocular proof of the courtier’s guilt, and causes him to be severely punished.

l: the story of Mars and Venus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_copied_by Ovid [from Homer’s version with a small variation] The story is described as a loose tale of the loves of Mars and Venus, contrasted with the affecting tale of Pyramus and Thisbe. Palæphatus says that Homer first related the fable, with a small variation, and that Ovid copied it; similarity of names helped give rise to it.

l: frankincense tree, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The frankincense tree, proposed as the natural subject symbolized by Leucothoë, grows from her dissolved body after the Sun sprinkles nectar on earth. Its shoot roots through clods and breaks a hillock, is odoriferous, produces an aromatic drug used in physic, and may be killed by a nearby sunflower.

l: sunflower, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The sunflower is a plant associated with Clytie’s metamorphosis after she pines away for the Sun. Rooted in the ground, it continues to turn toward the Sun and retain her passion. Some naturalists say it kills a nearby frankincense tree; Pliny recorded other properties.

l: Leucothoë's burial alive, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Leucothoë's burial alive is a story event attributed to her father Orchamus, who punishes her after learning of her affair with the Sun. He buries her deep in the ground under heavy sand as she reaches for light and says the Sun forced himself on her. It has no ascertained historical basis.

l: Leucothoë's transformation into frankincense, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: transforms Leucothoë The Sun cannot restore Leucothoë to life, so he sprinkles her body and the place with odoriferous nectar. Her body dissolves into fragrant juices, and a frankincense shoot grows from the earth.

l: Clytie's transformation into a sunflower, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Clytie's transformation into a sunflower is a story element, not an ascertained historical fact. After the Sun ends intercourse with her, she pines without food or water, survives on dew and tears, becomes rooted and pale, and changes into a flower that continually turns toward the Sun.

l: Clytie's betrayal, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Clytie, resentful of Leucothoë, reveals an affair to Leucothoë’s father; her betrayal leads to Leucothoë’s burial alive, though grief and love might have excused it.

l: the story of Leucothoë and Clytie, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_founded_on natural philosophy [most probably] The story concerns Leucothoë's burial alive by her father Orchamus after her love for Apollo and Clytie's transformation into a sunflower. The explanation finds no established historical basis for it and suggests that it was probably founded on natural philosophy.

l: Daphnis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Daphnis is a shepherd of Ida, associated with Crete or Phrygia. He has a Nymph as paramour and affronts Thalia. In the end, the Nymph’s resentment turns him into stone, an event also described as allegorically expressing insensibility.

l: Daphnis's transformation into a stone, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: A transformation in which Daphnis, resented by his paramour the Nymph, is turned into stone.

l: Scython, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Scython is said to have been first a man and then a woman after the law of nature was altered, changing to the opposite sex. The report may instead arise from Thrace, once called Scython, later taking a feminine name.

l: Scython's transformation from man into woman, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: A transformation in which Scython changes from a man into a woman after the law of nature is altered.

l: Celmus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Celmus is a remarkably wise, moderate young man, untouched by passions. Formerly attached to Jupiter in Jupiter’s youth, he is said to have been Jupiter’s foster-father. His resistance to passion changes him into adamant; in another account, Jupiter encloses him in an impenetrable tower for revealing the immortality of the Gods.

l: Celmus's transformation into adamant, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: A transformation in which Celmus is changed into adamant, beginning and ending with that change.

l: Curetes, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The Curetes are described as ancient inhabitants of Crete, said to emerge from a plenteous shower of rain and to descend from Uranus and Tita. They watch over Jupiter during his infancy, later conceal Epaphus from Jupiter's wrath, and are slain by Jupiter for doing so.

l: Curetes' emergence from a shower of rain, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Curetes emerge from a plenteous shower of rain.

l: Crocus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Crocus is a youth associated with Smilax in accounts of their transformation into little flowers. One account makes them constantly and happily married; another has Crocus reject Smilax’s advances. In both, their chaste, innocent, or otherwise linked lives end with both changed into flowers.

l: Smilax, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Smilax is likely a Nymph associated with a herb, though the word may also denote a yew or oak. In accounts involving Crocus, Smilax is changed into a little flower: either as part of a chaste married couple or after loving Crocus and being rejected.

l: Crocus and Smilax's transformation into flowers, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: A transformation changes Crocus and Smilax together into little flowers.

l: Thalia, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_a Nymph Thalia was the Nymph whom Daphnis affronted. The account connects her story with Daphnis being turned into stone.

l: Caria, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Caria, a province adjoining Lycia, contains a fountain near Halicarnassus associated with men’s reputed transformation into women.

l: the fountain of Salmacis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The fountain is a clear, walled pool in Lycia or neighboring Caria, edged by green turf and ever-verdant grass without reeds or rushes. Salmacis dwells there. Its well-known but unexplained, enervating waters are later tainted with ambiguous drugs; it civilizes barbarians and gains a reputation for changing men into women, perhaps through nearby disgraceful adventures.

l: water of the fountain near Halicarnassus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Clear, pleasantly tempered fountain water becomes, after Hermaphroditus's parents grant his request, enfeebling: men entering emerge half men and become effeminate when touched. Displaced barbarians use it, while its unusual effects may reflect a peculiar chemical quality.

l: the transformation of Salmacis and Hermaphroditus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The Gods unite Salmacis and Hermaphroditus after her prayer, transforming their two bodies into one human shape retaining both sexes, both and neither woman nor boy.

l: the fountain's enervating power, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The fountain’s infamous power enervates and softens bathers’ limbs through its waters; its cause is unknown, though the waters acquire it after Hermaphroditus’s parents taint them with drugs of ambiguous quality.

l: Halicarnassus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Halicarnassus is the town near which, in Caria, the reputedly transformative fountain was located.

l: Argive colony, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: drives_out barbarians [from the neighborhood of the fountain] The Argive colony was established near the fountain and drove certain barbarians from the neighborhood.

l: Greek colonists, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: meet barbarians [at the fountain] Greek colonists encountered the displaced barbarians at the fountain when both groups went there for water. Their intercourse civilized the barbarians but also corrupted them by introducing the luxurious manners of Greece.

l: barbarians, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Barbarians, driven from the neighborhood by the Argive colony, seek water at a fountain near Halicarnassus, meet Greek colonists, and adopt polished, luxurious Greek manners.

l: luxurious manners of Greece, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The luxurious manners of Greece were introduced to the barbarians through their intercourse with the Greek colonists. They are described as corrupting the barbarians even while Greek contact civilized them.

l: chemical quality of the water, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: causes effeminacy caused by the fountain [possibly, among those who drank the water] A peculiar chemical quality of the water is proposed as a possible explanation for the fountain’s extraordinary effects. Such a quality might have made those who drank it soft and effeminate.

l: effeminacy caused by the fountain, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The fountain was reputed to make men into women, possibly because its water made drinkers soft and effeminate. This explanation is presented as a possibility rather than a certainty.

l: the daughters' work, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The daughters’ work continues as Bacchus transforms webs and cloth into green foliage, ivy, vines, and grapes.

l: webs, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: become ivy [green and leafy] The webs begin to grow green and put forth foliage like ivy. Parts of them change into vines, and their former threads become vine shoots.

l: cloth, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Cloth hanging in the loom puts forth ivy-like foliage, partly changes into vines; purple lends splendor to tinted grapes.

l: ivy, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Ivy foliage grows from the cloth and webs as the transformation begins.

l: vines, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: bear grapes [tinted and purple] Vines arise from parts of the transformed work, with vine branches springing from the warp.

l: the house, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: A smoking house shakes as torches and fires blaze, beasts howl, and daughters of Minyas hide during transformation.

l: dubious night, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_a time_between_darkness_and_light [at its commencement] Dubious night begins after the day has passed, at a time that can be called neither darkness nor light. It arrives together with the remaining light.

l: darkness, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Darkness accompanies the transformation and prevents the daughters from knowing how they have lost their former shape. The transformed creatures avoid the light and fly abroad by night.

l: light, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Light remains during the beginning of dubious night, while torches and fires illuminate the house. The transformed creatures abhor the light.

l: bats, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Bats, changed from Minyas’s daughters, have pellucid light wings, squeak, avoid light, frequent houses, and fly late evening.

l: transformation of the daughters of Minyas into bats, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The daughters of Minyas hide from fires and light, then membranes and wings transform them into squeaking bats that fly by night.

l: νυκτερίδες, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: νυκτερίδες is a Greek name, derived from νυξ, meaning “night.”

l: vespertiliones, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Vespertiliones is their Latin name, derived from vesper, “evening,” because of their habits.

l: Learchus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Learchus, infant son of Athamas and Ino, smiles in Ino’s arms before maddened Athamas seizes, whirls, and kills him after discovering Ino’s deception.

l: Cerberus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Cerberus, an Echidnean dog with three heads or three simultaneous barks, guards the gates and portals of the Infernal Regions. Homer calls it a dog, while Pausanias describes a serpent. Hercules drags it from Tartarus through Acherusia in chains; it barks furiously and scatters white foam. Its name means “one that devours flesh,” and its foam was believed to poison herbs and produce aconite.

l: Palæmon, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Palæmon, formerly Melicerta, becomes a sea deity after Neptune transforms him following a fall into the sea, then establishes the Isthmian games.

l: Sidonian attendants of Ino, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: serve Ino [as attendants] The Sidonian attendants follow Ino's footprints to the edge of the rock and, believing Ino and Melicerta dead, lament the house of Cadmus and reproach Juno. Juno transforms them according to their positions: some become fixed in stone and others become birds that skim over the sea.

l: Palace of Athamas, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Juno desires that the Palace of Athamas and the house of Cadmus should not stand. Tisiphone reaches the palace, where her arrival is marked by terror, shaking door-posts, and paleness on the door.

l: the Molarian rock, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: overhangs Ionian sea [rugged summit projecting over the open sea] The rock above the sea is worn hollow at its lower part by the waves, while its rugged summit projects over the open sea. Ino climbs it and casts herself and Melicerta into the deep.

l: Juno's poisoning of Athamas and Ino, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_a act of divine vengeance [carried out through Tisiphone] Juno's poisoning of Athamas and Ino is carried out by Tisiphone, who throws a mixture of poison, Cerberus's foam, Echidna's venom, rage, tears, crime, and the love of murder into their breasts. The poison attacks their minds rather than their limbs and produces their direful actions.

l: Athamas's killing of Learchus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_a act committed in madness Athamas's killing of Learchus occurs while Athamas is mad and mistakes Ino and her children for a lioness and her cubs. He seizes Learchus from Ino, whirls him around, and dashes him to pieces against the stones.

l: Ino and Melicerta's transformation into sea deities, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: A divine transformation in which, after Ino and Melicerta fall from a rock into the sea, Venus intercedes and Neptune removes their mortality, changes their forms and names to Leucothoë and Palæmon, and makes them sea deities, consoling their relatives after their deaths.

l: transformation of Ino's attendants, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: A divine punishment imposed by Juno after Ino's attendants blame her: they become stone in their postures or birds skimming over the sea.

l: madness, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Madness is brought to Athamas and Ino by Tisiphone's poison. It drives Athamas to kill Learchus and causes Ino to flee with Melicerta and leap into the sea.

l: Phryxus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Phryxus, child of Nephele and Athamas and brother of Helle, flees Ino's designs with Helle by ship. After Helle dies, he reaches Colchis, where Æetes receives him kindly and he marries Chalciope. Some years later Æetes kills him; his death prompts the Greek expedition.

l: Helle, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Nephele's daughter and Phryxus's sister travels with him by ship toward Colchis, falls overboard or dies during passage, and gives the Hellespont its name.

l: Æetes, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Æetes, son of Sun, is king of Colchis, father of Medea, and kinsman of Phryxus. After causing Phryxus’s assassination, he seizes Athamas’s treasures and, fearing an oracle, establishes stranger sacrifice. When Jason seeks the Golden Fleece, Æetes demands dangerous labors before granting it.

l: the famine at Thebes, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_caused_by Ino [according to the myth] The famine at Thebes was attributed to Ino's order that seed be parched before sowing. Athamas sought an oracle's guidance about it, and the response called for the sacrifice of Nephele's children.

l: the sacrifice of Nephele's children, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_ordered_by the oracle of Delphi [as the remedy for the famine] The sacrifice of Nephele's children was presented as the means of ending the famine at Thebes. The oracle's message was obtained after the priests were allegedly bribed or the messengers corrupted, but Phryxus was warned and escaped with Helle.

l: Phryxus and Helle's voyage to Colchis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Phryxus and Helle flee Ino's designs toward Colchis; Helle dies or falls en route, while Phryxus arrives and is welcomed by Æetes.

l: Ino's suicide, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_a suicide by drowning Ino's suicide occurred when she fled from Athamas after he killed Learchus and pursued her for revenge. Carrying Melicerta, she threw herself from a rock into the sea.

l: the explanation of the myth, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_based_on historical facts [according to Herodotus, Diodorus Siculus, and Pausanias] The explanation of the myth presents the story as possibly based on historical facts reported by Herodotus, Diodorus Siculus, and Pausanias. It connects the deaths and transformations of Ino and Melicerta with their later worship, the Isthmian games, and Roman religious practices.

l: Cadmus and Hermione as serpents, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Cadmus and Hermione become two joined serpents, enter an adjacent grove’s covert, remember what they were, and remain gentle toward humans.

l: Cadmus's exile and wandering, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_caused_by the calamities of Cadmus's family [along with sorrow and prodigies] Cadmus is forced to leave Thebes and wanders for a long time with his exiled wife. Their wandering ends when they reach the coast of Illyria.

l: transformation of Cadmus and Hermione into serpents, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Cadmus and Hermione become serpents in Illyria. Cadmus first lengthens, grows scales and azure spots, and loses human form; Hermione asks the Gods to transform her likewise, and they enter a nearby grove together. The account is presented as invented after Cadmus’s death and possibly based on his Phoenician origin.

l: the calamities of Cadmus's family, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The calamities of Cadmus's family, together with sorrow and numerous prodigies, drive him from Thebes. While in Illyria, Cadmus and Hermione recount the misfortunes of their house.

l: serpent, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Chiva was identified as a Hebrew and perhaps Phoenician word for serpent. The Greeks also called the ancient inhabitants of Illyria serpents and basilisks.

l: Phoenician origin of Cadmus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_a proposed explanation [for the serpent transformation story] Cadmus's Phoenician origin was proposed as a basis for the story that he and Hermione became serpents. Bochart connected the name Cadmus with Cadmonia, the eastern part of Phoenicia.

l: Enchelians, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: wage war between the Enchelians and Illyrians [against the Illyrians, with Cadmus's assistance] The Enchelians received Cadmus's assistance in their war against the Illyrians. After the Illyrians were defeated, they gave the crown to Cadmus.

l: Illyrians, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Illyrians are defeated by the Enchelians with Cadmus's assistance, give their crown to Cadmus for peace, and are associated by Greeks with serpents and basilisks.

l: war between the Enchelians and Illyrians, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Cadmus assisted the Enchelians in their war against the Illyrians. The Illyrians were defeated, and they gave the crown to Cadmus in order to obtain peace.

l: Gorgon’s head, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Gorgon’s head is Medusa’s snake-bearing head, cut from her neck by Perseus while she slept and carried as his memorable spoil after victory. Its most important power is petrification: in the fable, those who look at it become stone. Perseus sets it face-down on sea plants, whose poisonous touch changes them into coral. When surrounded by Phineus and a thousand followers, he reveals it, petrifying many attackers and finally Phineus; he also exposes it to Atlas, transforming Atlas into a mountain. It is said to produce serpents when Medusa’s bloody drops reach the ground. Notes interpret its effects as fear caused by Perseus’s fame or display of the head.

l: Perseus's birth, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_caused_by Danaë’s seduction by Jupiter [in the mythic account] Perseus was born to Danaë after her confinement by Acrisius. Acrisius then exposed Danaë and Perseus in a boat, but they survived after reaching Seriphus, where Polydectes received them.

l: Perseus's killing of Medusa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Perseus’s killing of Medusa is Medusa’s death, later explained as her defeat by Perseus. He and companions may surprise Medusa and her escort at night, or he acts after seizing her sisters’ minister and golden statue. Using Minerva’s reflecting shield to avoid looking directly at her, Perseus takes Medusa by the hair and cuts off her head. He carries it as spoil; its blood produces serpents in Libya, and its face petrifies Polydectes, proving the death was real.

l: Atlas's transformation, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: changes Atlas [into a mountain] Atlas's transformation occurs when Perseus exposes the Gorgon’s head to him. Atlas’s beard and hair become woods, his shoulders and hands become mountain ridges, his head becomes the mountain’s summit, and his bones become stones.

l: the oracle concerning Atlas's golden fruit, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The oracle given by the Parnassian Themis foretells Atlas’s tree stripped of gold and a son of Jupiter winning the prize, prompting Atlas to enclose his orchard and expel strangers.

l: golden apples, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Golden apples grow on gold-leaved, gold-branched trees in Atlas's enclosed orchard, guarded by a dragon and Atlas. Atlas fears their theft by a son of Jupiter, as foretold; they are also interpreted as gold mines, sheep, or hot-climate fruits.

l: Atlas's mountain form, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Atlas’s immense mountain, made of woods, ridges, stones, and summit, supports the whole heaven, with its many stars resting upon it.

l: Gorgons, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The Gorgons are a group variously described as female warriors near Lake Tritonis, wild women, wealthy sisters, beautiful women whose appearance petrifies, or a deadly animal. They are said to be daughters of Phorcus or Phorcys, numbering three in one account and two sisters in another, with shared possessions including islands, a golden statue of Minerva, a minister, and an eye of the Graeae. They inhabit Gorgades, possibly Cape Verde Islands. In the opening, Perseus reaches their fortified abode beneath Atlas and finds Medusa’s victims turned to stone.

l: Danaë’s seduction by Jupiter, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Danaë’s seduction by Jupiter is a mythic event in which Jupiter reaches Danaë as a shower of gold; a rationalizing account attributes access to Prœtus bribing guards.

l: Pegasus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Pegasus is a winged horse sprung from Medusa's blood; with his hard hoof, he opens the new fountain at Mount Helicon and is interpreted as ships.

l: Perseus myth interpretations, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The unit presents rationalizations of Perseus’s birth, his killing of Medusa, the petrifying power of Medusa’s head, the transformation of Atlas, Pegasus, and the golden apples. These interpretations connect the myths with political events, military exploits, voyages, geography, wealth, animals, and distinctive natural products.

l: Gorgon myth interpretations, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The Gorgon myths are interpreted as accounts of female warriors, savage women, wealthy sisters with a shared minister, beautiful women whose appearance caused astonishment, or a deadly animal. The sisters’ single eye may represent their shared minister, while Medusa’s petrifying head may represent a statue, terror, or the fame of Perseus’s exploits.

l: Atlas transformed into a mountain, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_a mountain Atlas has been changed into a mountain before Perseus proceeds to Æthiopia.

l: Cepheus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Cepheus, son of Phœnix, is Andromeda’s father and king of Joppa. With Cassiope he mourns her danger, accepts Perseus’s condition, promises a kingdom as dowry, and welcomes Perseus as son-in-law and preserver of their house. He later rebukes Phineus’s attack on Perseus, invoking justice, good faith, and hospitality; his memory and Phineus’s are honored at Joppa.

l: Cassiope, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Andromeda's mother boasts of beauty against the Nereids, causing punishment; she mourns at the rock, then rejoices when Perseus rescues Andromeda.

l: Andromeda's exposure to the sea monster, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Andromeda is bound to a hard rock and exposed to an approaching sea monster, ordered by Ammon as punishment for her mother’s boast comparing her beauty to the Nereids. Her parents lament helplessly until Perseus intervenes; the exposure is also interpreted as forced betrothal for Cepheus’s realms’ safety.

l: sea monster, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The sea monster is a sea monster with a fish tail, sent by Neptune at the Nereids’ request against the Ethiopians and destined to devour the exposed Andromeda. It rises from the ocean and advances on her, but Perseus confronts it, wounds it repeatedly with his sword, and kills it by thrusting the sword through its entrails. Its skeleton was reportedly displayed by Joppa’s inhabitants.

l: Perseus's rescue of Andromeda, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_achieved_by Perseus [through valor] Perseus offers to save Andromeda in exchange for marriage, then attacks the sea monster from the air and kills it. Andromeda is released from her chains and becomes the reward and cause of his labor.

l: nuptials of Perseus and Andromeda, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Perseus and Andromeda marry after the rescue without a dowry, celebrating with Hymenaeus, Cupid, music, perfumes, garlands, and feast.

l: coral, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Coral is a sea plant that becomes stone and hardens in air after leaving the sea; its production may be explained by the defeat of the Gorgons.

l: transformation of sea plants into coral, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_caused_by Gorgon’s head [through contact with its poison] Sea plants placed beneath Medusa's head absorb its poison and harden. The sea Nymphs repeat the experiment, and the text says that plants in the sea become coral when removed from it and exposed to air.

l: Medusa's beheading, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Perseus beheads Medusa while she and her serpents sleep, using his bronze shield’s reflection; Pegasus emerges from her blood.

l: Medusa's serpents, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Serpents mingle with Medusa's hair and sleep during Perseus's attack, then are borne by Minerva on her breast to terrify foes.

l: Medusa's transformation of hair into serpents, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_caused_by Minerva [as punishment for the desecration of her temple] Medusa's hair is transformed into hideous snakes by Minerva. The transformation occurs after Neptune violates Medusa in Minerva's temple, and the snakes become a source of terror to Medusa's foes.

l: Joppa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_alternative_name_for Jaffa [a city] Joppa, or Jaffa, is identified by Josephus and Strabo as the place near which the event involving Andromeda occurred. Pomponius Mela calls Cepheus its king and says that its inhabitants honored Cepheus and Phineus and displayed the bones of the monster.

l: victory over the Gorgons, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The victory over the Gorgons is said to have caused widespread terror and to have contributed to reports that Perseus could petrify his enemies by displaying the Gorgon’s head.

l: petrification of Phineus and his followers, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: A fabled petrification: Perseus reveals the Gorgon, turning Phineus’s followers into rigid stone; Phineus sees his petrified friends, begs for the head’s removal, and is transformed into a stone statue.

l: interpretation of the Andromeda myth, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The explanation proposes that the Andromeda story may preserve an account of a pirate prince, a forced betrothal, and Perseus’s defeat of the pirate. It also suggests that Phineus may have been the enemy from whom Andromeda was rescued, or that the sea monster may have been the name of the ship intended to carry her away.

l: Medusa’s petrifying gaze, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The petrifying power associated with Medusa’s gaze turns people who behold the Gorgon head into stone. It affects enemies and also accidentally petrifies Aconteus, a soldier fighting for Perseus.

l: Phineus’s attack, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: occurs_at battle at the wedding feast [during the marriage celebration] Phineus’s attack begins when he rushes into the palace with his adherents and attempts to kill Perseus. His spear misses Perseus and kills Rhœtus instead, after which the fighting spreads throughout the wedding feast.

l: battle at the wedding feast, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_fought_between Perseus and Phineus [with Phineus and his adherents attacking Perseus] The wedding celebration becomes a violent battle between Perseus and Phineus’s followers. Numerous combatants are killed by swords, spears, and improvised weapons, while Pallas protects and encourages Perseus. The battle ends when Perseus displays the Gorgon head and petrifies many of the combatants.

l: story of Andromeda, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: has_possible_source Jonah [some authors suggest a confused version of the story] The story of Andromeda is placed by some accounts in Æthiopia, but the explanation considers the coast of Africa near Joppa more likely. It concerns Andromeda’s fastening to a rock and the monster that was supposed to devour her.

l: alleged metamorphoses into stone, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The alleged metamorphoses into stone are explained as stories arising from Perseus’s reputed use of the Gorgon’s head against his enemies. Bochart further supposes that the rocky character of Seriphus helped produce these traditions.

l: heroism of Perseus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: causes terror [everywhere, according to the explanation] The heroism of Perseus is presented as the probable reality behind the claim that he could turn enemies into stone. His fame and victories were said to create such consternation that the metaphor was reported as a literal power.

l: fountain of Pegasus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_opened_by Pegasus [with his hard hoof] The fountain of Pegasus was opened by the hard hoof of Pegasus, who sprang from the blood of Medusa. Minerva visits it and admires its waters.

l: death of Pyreneus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_a death [caused by his fall from the tower] After the Muses flew away, Pyreneus climbed onto the top of his house and tried to follow them. He threw himself from the tower, fell on his face, and broke the bones of his skull, dying in his own blood.

l: magpies, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Magpies are nine birds, transformed from the Pierides or Emathian sisters after defeat in a dispute. In woods and groves, they perch on lofty branches or hang in the air, lamenting their fate while retaining garrulity, chattering, and imitation with distinct human-like voices.

l: Pierus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Pierus is a very bad poet whose injurious, idle, tiresome, and unmeaning narratives include a work on the war of the Gods with the Giants; he is father of the Pierides, whose transformation into magpies represents his narratives.

l: contest between the Muses and the Emathian sisters, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: A contest of words, voice, and skill pits the Pierides, or Emathian sisters, against the Muses before Nymph judges. After a Pierides sings of the Gods’ flight from Typhoeus, the Muses answer; the Nymphs award victory to the Goddesses of Helicon, and the abusive losers are punished.

l: Calliope, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Calliope, the greatest Muse, is chosen to lead the Muses in a singing contest with the Pierides; ivy-haired, she tunes her lyre, sings the Muses’ song, and finishes it.

l: song of Calliope, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Calliope’s learned song begins after she tunes and accompanies herself on a lyre, singing with its struck strings; it tells of Ceres, Triptolemus, and Lyncus, then ends before the Nymphs judge the contest.

l: learning, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_taught_in institutions Learning is represented as something opposed by Pyreneus, who allegedly destroyed institutions in which it was taught. The Muses’ adventure with Pyreneus is explained as an allegory of this hostility.

l: the Muses' adventure with Pyreneus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_a metaphor [about Pyreneus's hostility to learning] The adventure is interpreted by Plutarch as a metaphor for Pyreneus’s opposition to learning. The associated story says that the Muses asked the Gods for wings to save themselves and that Pyreneus lost his life pursuing them.

l: the challenge given by the Pierides to the Muses, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_first_mentioned_by Ovid [no earlier writer is said to mention it] The challenge is said not to appear in any writer before Ovid. It is explained through the claim that Pierus was a poor poet whose irreverent and meaningless stories became associated with his daughters’ transformation into magpies.

l: Pluto's survey of Sicily, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_a survey [of the foundations of the Sicilian land] Pluto's survey of Sicily begins after Typhœus's struggles make him fear that the earth may open and expose the trembling ghosts to daylight. Riding in a chariot drawn by black horses, he cautiously examines the foundations of the island and sets aside his fear once he finds no insecure place.

l: Cupid's wounding of Pluto, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Cupid bends his flexible bow by pressing his knee against it and strikes Pluto in the breast with a barbed arrow. The attack follows Erycina's command that Cupid extend their influence over Tartarus.

l: natural phenomena, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: are_explained_by fabulous grounds [by the ancients] The ancients frequently explained natural phenomena through fabulous or supernatural causes when they could not account for them through natural philosophy.

l: Enceladus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_buried_under Ætna [according to some authors] According to some authors, Enceladus took the place of Typhœus in the story of the defeated giant buried beneath Mount Ætna. His attempts to escape the mountain’s weight were believed to cause fires and earthquakes.

l: volcanic eruptions, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: are_caused_by internal fires of Ætna [according to the explanation] The ancients attributed volcanic eruptions to the struggles of Typhœus or Enceladus beneath Mount Ætna. The explanation notes that Ætna contains sulphur and bituminous matter that could provide a natural source for its eruptions.

l: earthquakes, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: are_caused_by internal fires of Ætna [when struggling for a vent] Earthquakes were attributed in the fable to the attempts of Typhœus or Enceladus to free himself from Mount Ætna. The explanation instead refers to the forces of Ætna’s internal fires struggling for a vent.

l: Stellio, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Stellio, an impudent, bold boy who mocks Ceres drinking barley liquor, is sprinkled with the remaining drink and becomes a diminutive, spotted newt.

l: newt (Stellio), The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_a newt [smaller than a small lizard and speckled] The transformed Stellio has a contracted face, legs in place of arms, a tail, and a body smaller than a small lizard. He bears various spots, flees from the old woman, and seeks a hiding place.

l: abduction of Proserpine, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The abduction of Proserpine is an event in which Pluto forcibly carries Proserpina away while she gathers violets and white lilies near Henna in Sicily. She cries for Ceres and her companions as he drives through lakes, sulfurous pools, and a passage toward Tartarus. Ceres learns of it from Proserpine’s girdle and Arethusa, calls it an outrage, and asks Jupiter for her daughter’s return.

l: Cyane's transformation into a fountain, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: A transformation caused by grief and anguish: after Pluto disregards her, Cyane mourns Proserpina and her spring until her body dissolves into ungraspable pure water, becoming a fountain.

l: Ceres's search for Proserpina, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Ceres searches throughout lands and seas for Proserpina, traveling from sunrise to sunset without rest or an immediate answer. Carrying burning pine torches, she becomes thirsty and receives barley liquor from an old woman at a thatched cottage. The search reaches Sicily, near Italy’s coast, where Cyane’s girdle and Arethusa’s testimony reveal Proserpine’s location. The Sirens are associated with conducting or aiding the search, possibly by ship.

l: transformation of Stellio, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Stellio mocks Ceres while she drinks; she sprinkles him with barley and liquor, transforming him into a small, spotted newt-like creature, possibly a poet’s fancy.

l: Syracuse, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: has two harbors [one much larger than the other] Syracuse is described as a city founded by Archias of the Bacchiadae and as having two harbors. According to the account associated with Henna, Pluto descended into the earth not far from Syracuse, where a lake arose and an annual festival was celebrated.

l: Eleusis, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Eleusis, in Attica and dedicated especially to Ceres, is where she rested while seeking Proserpine; Triptolemus reigned there, established Ceres’s mysteries and worship, and Eumolpus held religious office.

l: Aidoneus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_a king of Epirus [according to Le Clerc] Aidoneus is presented as a possible historical ruler of Epirus or king of the Molossians who was later confused with Pluto. The account suggests that he may have ordered pirates to seize Proserpine and carry her toward Epirus.

l: rape of Proserpine, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The rape of Proserpine is a story associated by many authors with Henna and involving Pluto. It may preserve natural philosophy, ancient history, or both: Pluto's seizure of Proserpine is variously explained through pirates acting for Aidoneus, mining regions ruled by Pluto, buried grain, or Erectheus's intended sacrifice of his daughter.

l: worship of Ceres, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The worship of Ceres was highly esteemed at Henna, whose inhabitants were regarded as her priests. Probably imported from Egypt as a mysterious worship, it later became connected with agriculture, the Earth, and civil order, while Triptolemus carried it to different countries.

l: Eleusinian mysteries, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The Eleusinian mysteries were rites of Ceres, brought from Egypt and instituted at Eleusis by Triptolemus during his reign. They may have accompanied the introduction of Ceres’s mysterious worship and had already been introduced into Sicily, supporting the tradition of Ceres coming from Sicily to Athens.

l: famine in Greece, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: occurred_during_reign_of Erectheus A famine in Greece during the reign of Erectheus led the Greeks to seek corn from Egypt. The crisis encouraged them to adopt the worship of the agricultural deity and helped form the explanation of Ceres and Proserpine’s story.

l: Proserpine’s girdle, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Proserpine’s girdle is a fastening worn around the loins to hold up a tunic, sometimes money or a purse, and part of a warrior’s cuirass. Worn by both sexes, young women discontinued it at marriage. It falls into Cyane’s sacred stream; Cyane shows it, Ceres recognizes it, and its continued wearing indicates violence against Proserpine.

l: pomegranate, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: A pomegranate grows on a bending tree in a finely cultivated garden, enclosing seeds within a pale rind. Proserpine plucks it and eats seven grains, causing her partial stay in the Infernal Regions; it is thereafter avoided during Ceres’ rites.

l: pomegranate seeds, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Proserpine eats seven pomegranate seeds while walking in the garden. Their consumption prevents her complete return to heaven under the law of the Destinies.

l: owl, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Owl, a tawny-winged bird formed when Proserpine changes Ascalaphus, foretells approaching woe as a direful omen to mortals.

l: agriculture and fertility, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_ruined_in Sicily [after Ceres’s anger] Ceres’s anger causes the fertility of Sicily to be ruined. Corn dies, seed is spoiled, and heat, rain, winds, constellations, birds, darnel, thistles, and weeds damage the crops.

l: Proserpine’s return to the upper world, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Jupiter agrees that Proserpine may return to heaven if she has eaten no food in the Infernal Regions. Her eating of seven pomegranate seeds prevents the return permitted by that condition.

l: Ascalaphus’s punishment and transformation, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Ascalaphus’s punishment and transformation follows his revealing that Proserpine ate pomegranate seeds. Proserpine changes him: his head becomes a beak, feathers, and large eyes, his body gains tawny wings, and he becomes a sluggish owl. Accounts also describe him as a lizard, linked to his death in Pluto’s mines and his name.

l: the law of the Destinies, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: requires Proserpine’s return to the upper world [only if she has touched no food in the Infernal Regions] The law of the Destinies provides that Proserpine may return only if she has touched no food in the Infernal Regions. Because she has eaten pomegranate seeds, the condition is not fulfilled.

l: the pomegranate eating, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: affects Proserpine’s return to the upper world [by preventing it] While walking innocently in a cultivated garden, Proserpine plucks a pomegranate and chews seven grains from it. Ascalaphus witnesses the act and reports it, preventing her return to heaven.

l: treaty concerning Proserpine, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: A treaty concerning Proserpine divides her residence between Ceres on earth and Pluto in the Infernal Regions: Apollodorus assigns nine months to Ceres and three to Pluto, while other writers give each six months.

l: the division of the year between Ceres and Pluto, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_a equal division of the rolling year Jupiter divides the rolling year equally between Ceres and Pluto. Ceres's daughter consequently spends equal numbers of months with her mother and her husband.

l: the passion of Alpheus for Arethusa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: A poetic romantic pursuit in which Alpheus chases Arethusa after she flees her bathing stream, following her across distant regions and beneath the sea. Diana hides Arethusa in a cloud, but Alpheus continues searching; the story was considered a fable by Pausanias.

l: Arethusa's transformation into a fountain, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_a transformation [of Arethusa into a stream] While concealed and besieged by fear, Arethusa begins to shed water from her body, and wherever she steps a lake flows. She is changed into a stream, while Alpheus becomes water and attempts to mingle with her.

l: Fountain of Arethusa, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Fountain of Arethusa, surrounded by willows, was named Alphaga by Phoenicians for “the fountain of the willows” or “a stream”; Greeks later misread this as Alpheus.

l: lynx, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_a animal [the transformed Lyncus] The lynx is the form into which Ceres transforms Lyncus when he tries to attack Triptolemus.

l: Nymphs, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: declare_winners Goddesses of Helicon [with unanimous voice] The Nymphs unanimously declare that the Goddesses of Helicon have won the contest. They witness the punishment of the defeated Emathian sisters.

l: Emathian sisters, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The Emathian sisters lose a contest to the Muses, then abuse their opponents and despise threatening language. Punished after their defeat, they transform as feathers grow from their nails and arms, their faces become hard beaks, and they become magpies.

l: punishment of the Emathian sisters, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: transforms Emathian sisters [into magpies] The Emathian sisters are transformed into birds after abusing the victors. Their punishment leaves them with their original talkativeness, jarring garrulity, and great love of chattering.

l: Eumolpus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Eumolpus, a Hierophant and early initiate into Ceres's mysteries, wages war against Erectheus and is killed in battle; afterward, his descendants retain the office.

l: Eleusinians, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The Eleusinians fought against Erectheus, king of Athens. Their conflict ended with Eumolpus and Erectheus being killed in battle.

l: Hierophant, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_held_by descendants of Eumolpus [in future] The Hierophant was the explainer of the mysteries of Eleusis. Eumolpus held this office, and after his death it was retained by his descendants.

l: war between Eumolpus and Erectheus, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_between Erectheus [Eumolpus made war against him] Eumolpus made war against Erectheus, king of Athens. The war ended with both of them being killed in battle, after which their descendants received separate hereditary roles.

l: battle between the Eleusinians and Athenians, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The battle between the Eleusinians and Athenians resulted in the deaths of Eumolpus and Erectheus. It was then agreed that Erectheus's descendants would rule Athens and Eumolpus's descendants would retain the office of Hierophant.

l: Arachne's transformation into a spider, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Arachne’s transformation into a spider is a divine punishment inflicted by Minerva after Arachne hangs herself. Minerva keeps her alive, decrees that she and her descendants will hang, and sprinkles her with a noxious herb. Arachne’s features vanish, her body shrinks, her fingers become legs, and she produces thread and weaves as a spider.

l: the weaving contest, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_a contest of skill [in weaving and working wool] Minerva and Arachne weave separate webs using fine warp, woof, shuttles, and vivid colors. Minerva depicts the contest between Neptune and herself for the city and adds examples of mortals punished for challenging the gods. Arachne depicts Europa and numerous divine transformations and deceptions, producing work that Minerva cannot blame for its craftsmanship.

l: the spider, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: The spider is Arachne transformed by Minerva, giving forth thread and weaving webs as she formerly wove.

l: Pygmies, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: Pygmies are a supposedly diminutive people described by ancient writers, variously placed in Ethiopia, India, Scythia, and parts of Africa, and traditionally said to wage continual warfare with Cranes; later explanations seek a historical or natural basis for this story.

l: Arachne’s challenge, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_based_on competition [over the merit of inventing textile arts] Arachne’s challenge is explained as a competition over the merit of inventing or mastering textile arts, especially the working of silk and wool. The contest allows Ovid to contrast Arachne’s human skill with Minerva’s divine status.

l: dispute between Neptune and Minerva, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: concerns Athens [over giving the city its name] The dispute concerns the right to name or claim patronage over Athens. Minerva’s olive tree was judged more useful than Neptune’s gift, which was variously understood as a fountain, a horse, or possibly a ship; later explanations connect the myth with the transition from piracy to agriculture and civilized life.

l: weaving and textile artistry, The Metamorphoses of Ovid, Books I-VII
s: is_associated_with Arachne [working in silk and wool] Weaving and textile artistry form the basis of Arachne’s reputation and her challenge to Minerva. Arachne is credited in the explanation with exceptional skill in silk and wool, while Pliny is said to have reported that she invented linen cloths and nets, though some attributed that invention to Minerva.
